title: Deck and fence scope, permits and boundary survey
audience: Deck and fence maintenance workers and the people who scope and quote deck and fence work
learningOutcomes: Identify when a deck or fence needs a building permit, a planning approval or a licensed contractor, by state.
Confirm property boundaries and the owner's authority before a deck or fence is set out.
Refer permit, planning and boundary questions and record the referral.

instruction.heading: Three separate questions
instruction.body: Deck and fence jobs raise three questions that are easy to mix up. The first is whether a building permit or planning approval applies. The second is whether the work is licensed work, so that the person doing it must hold a particular licence. The third is where the property boundary sits, and whether the owner has the right to build on that line. The answers come from different sources. A deck can be exempt from planning and still need a licensed contractor, and a fence can need no permit while being in dispute at the boundary. Answer each question separately, write down the source for each answer, and keep the answers apart in the job file. A single 'yes, it's fine' is not a usable record.

instruction.heading: Victoria: permits for decks and fences
instruction.body: The Victorian Building Authority practice note on building permits sets out the rules for decks, verandahs and fences. An attached deck needs a building permit irrespective of its size, and a detached deck that forms part of the amenity of a building also needs one. The size of the deck does not create an exemption for attached work, so a small deck still needs the permit position confirmed. For fences, the note exempts a fence that is not more than 2 metres high, but fences near a street are capped. Within 3 metres of a street, the limit is 1.5 metres for non-masonry fences and 1.2 metres for masonry or concrete fences. Within 9 metres of a street intersection, the limit is 1 metre above the footpath. Fences that form part of a pool barrier, and fences around children's outdoor play spaces, are outside the exemption. The cover of the note is dated April 2022, but its version history refers to a 2021 publication, so the current version must be checked before the note is relied on.

instruction.heading: New South Wales: exempt decks and fences
instruction.body: In New South Wales, exempt development rules set the limits within which a deck or fence needs no development approval. The planning page for decks and patios sets the top of an exempt deck at no more than 3 metres above existing ground at its highest point, and the floor no more than 1 metre above existing ground. The setback from the lot boundary is 5 metres in the listed rural and R5 zones and 900 millimetres in other zones. The structure must also not extend beyond the building line of a road frontage. For fences in the listed residential zones, a side or rear boundary fence must not exceed 1.8 metres, or 1.2 metres if it is built of masonry, and a fence along a primary or secondary road frontage must not exceed 1.2 metres. These are the exempt limits. A fence or deck above them, or outside a listed zone, needs the planning route that applies to the property. Check the zone for the property before relying on these numbers.

instruction.heading: Queensland and other states
instruction.body: Brisbane City Council states that building approval is needed for a fence more than 2 metres above the natural ground surface, measured across screens, fences and retaining walls combined. The page shows only a copyright year, so it is not dated. This rule applies to Brisbane only. Do not apply the Victorian or New South Wales limits to another state. Ask the local council or the building certifier, record the answer, and keep the source name and the date the answer was given.

instruction.heading: Boundary and the owner's authority
instruction.body: Before a deck or fence is set out, two things must be confirmed. The first is the owner's authority. The owner, or a person the owner has authorised in writing, must confirm the property address and the work to be done. The second is the boundary. Use the owner's title or survey documents to locate the boundary, and do not set out a line on the owner's word alone or from the position of an existing fence. Where a neighbour disputes the line, or where the documents are unclear, stop setting out and refer the question to a licensed surveyor or the owner's legal adviser. The record should show what was relied on for the boundary, not only that the boundary was marked.

instruction.heading: Licences are a separate question
instruction.body: A planning exemption does not change the licence position. In New South Wales, a contractor licence is needed for fencing work valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials, including GST, and the page applies this to fences regardless of materials. The deck licence question in New South Wales is covered in “Footings, post setting and levels”. In Queensland, the QBCC fence guide says a licence is not required for a fence on non-agricultural land valued under $3,300, and the QBCC licence page sets the same $3,300 figure for building work. These licence positions are explained further in “Footings, post setting and levels”. This lesson does not decide whether a particular contractor needs a licence. It asks that the question is asked, answered and recorded before work is quoted or started.

procedure: Record the property address, the owner's name and the owner's written authority for the deck or fence work.
Obtain the title or survey documents for the boundary, and identify the boundary markers on site. Do not set out until the position is confirmed from those documents.
Identify the state and the council, and record whether the deck is attached or detached, its height, and its distance from the boundary and any street.
Check the permit and planning position against the official source for that state or council, and record the source name and the page date.
Check the contractor licence position for the job separately, using the official source for the state, and record the answer.
Refer any permit, planning, licence or boundary question to the owner and to the relevant authority, such as the building surveyor, council or a licensed surveyor. Record the referral and the reply.
Hold the start of work until the referral has been answered and the answers are in the job file.

workedExamples.situation: An owner in Victoria wants a timber deck attached to the back of the house. The owner says the deck is small, so no approval is needed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Does the owner need a permit, and what is the first action?
workedExamples.reasoning: Yes, a building permit is needed. The practice note says an attached deck needs a permit irrespective of its size. The owner's view that the deck is small does not change that. Refer the permit question to the building surveyor or council, record the advice, and do not start the deck until the permit position is confirmed. Price the permit as a separate step so the owner can see the cost of compliance.

workedExamples.situation: An owner in a listed residential zone in New South Wales asks for a masonry fence on the side boundary, 1.5 metres high. This is an example job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the fence within the exempt limit?
workedExamples.reasoning: No, not on the exempt rule as written. The exempt limit for a side or rear boundary fence is 1.2 metres if it is built of masonry. A 1.5 metre masonry side fence is above that limit. Do not set out or quote it as exempt. Refer the design to the owner and the planning route for the property, and record the height and the zone used for the check.

workedExamples.situation: A neighbour says the proposed fence line is 300 millimetres inside the true boundary. The owner's documents show a different position. This example is for training.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do before any post is placed?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop setting out. Record the neighbour's statement and the documents relied on, and refer the question to a licensed surveyor or the owner's adviser. Post placement waits until the question is answered. The 300 millimetre figure is an example, not a measurement from a real site.

equipmentAndPpe: Owner's title, survey or boundary documents, with the owner's written authority
Measuring tape and a site plan for recording heights, setbacks and distances
Printed or saved copies of the state and council rules used for the check, with the page date
Closed footwear and a high-visibility vest for any site visit, although desk checks need no PPE
Survey pegs and line only after the boundary is confirmed

commonErrors.error: Assuming a small deck needs no permit.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the permit rule for the state. In Victoria, an attached deck needs a permit at any size.

commonErrors.error: Setting out a fence before the boundary is confirmed.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the boundary from the owner's documents, and stop and refer any dispute.

commonErrors.error: Treating a planning exemption as a licence exemption.
commonErrors.prevention: Answer the permit, the planning and the licence questions separately, each with its own source.

commonErrors.error: Relying on an old copy of a rule, or on another state's limits.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the official page for the state and council, check its date, and record the date in the job file.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Victoria registration threshold: domestic building work costing more than $10,000 needs registration as a registered building practitioner. Re-blocking, re-stumping or demolishing needs registration at any cost. Work above $10,000 needs that registration. This lesson does not give a registration or a building permit.

Victoria: an attached deck needs a building permit at any size, and a detached deck that forms part of a building's amenity needs one. A fence of up to 2 metres is exempt, subject to the street limits in the practice note. The note's cover is dated April 2022 and its version history says 2021, so confirm the current version.

New South Wales: exempt decks must stay within the height, floor-height and setback limits on the planning page, and exempt fences within the height limits for the zone. Both pages were updated on 23 March 2026. The planning exemption does not change the licence test for fencing work.
Queensland: Brisbane City Council requires building approval for a fence more than 2 metres above natural ground.

Completing this lesson does not give a building permit, a planning approval, a contractor licence, or authority to set out a boundary. Those come from the authority or licence holder, not from a course.

qualityStandard: The owner's written authority and the boundary source are confirmed before any line is set out.
The permit and planning position is checked for the state and council, with the source name and page date recorded.
The contractor licence position is checked separately, using the official source for the state, and recorded.
Every permit, planning, licence or boundary question is referred in writing, and the reply is filed before work starts.
documentationEvidence: Scope record showing the owner's written authority, the property address and the boundary source
Permit and planning check record with the state, council, source name, URL and page date
Licence check record for the job, with the source used
Referral note for each permit, planning or boundary question, with the reply
summary: Answer the permit, the licence and the boundary questions separately, each with its own source.
In Victoria an attached deck needs a building permit at any size, and fences have street-side height limits.
In New South Wales, exempt deck and fence limits are set by the planning pages, and fencing work over $5,000 including GST needs a licence.
Confirm the owner's authority and the boundary before setting out, and refer any dispute.

knowledgeChecks.question: In Victoria, an owner says a small attached deck needs no approval. What is correct?
options: It needs no approval because it is small, sits close to the house, and the owner has already checked it with the council
An attached deck needs a building permit at any size, so the permit position must be confirmed before work starts
Only decks that are not attached to the house need a permit, so this one is exempt from the check
Only the contractor decides whether a permit is needed, after the first site visit is complete and the quote is signed

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must the boundary be confirmed before a fence is set out?
options: Because the fence colour depends on the boundary line, the paint system and the owner's choice of finish on the day
Because fences are always placed on the boundary line, so the line is never checked on the site with the owner
Because setting out on the wrong line creates a dispute, and the owner's right to build on that line must be confirmed
It does not need to be confirmed if the owner is sure of the line and has walked it with the crew before the job starts

knowledgeChecks.question: In a listed New South Wales residential zone, an owner wants a masonry side fence 1.5 metres high under the exempt rules. What is correct?
options: It is exempt because 1.5 metres is under the general height limit of 1.8 metres for side fences in every residential zone in the state
It is not exempt on that basis, because the exempt limit for a masonry side or rear fence is lower, so the planning route must be checked
It is exempt if the neighbour agrees to the height in writing, since the neighbour is the one who shares the fence line
It is exempt only along the road frontage, where the height is set by the council for all fences and gates in the zone
